name: Predicting Proposal Success
title: Predicting Proposal Success
answer: Predicting proposal success is the use of statistical and machine learning models to estimate how likely a grant application is to be funded, or how it will score in review, before or alongside the actual review. It covers funder-specific prediction, such as forecasting panel outcomes for a given call, and cross-funder work that looks for general signals of a strong proposal. The unit of prediction is usually a single submitted proposal, though some work predicts at the level of a research team, a portfolio or a programme. It sits between bibliometrics, science of science research and the practical work of research development offices.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predicting proposal success is the use of statistical and machine learning models to estimate how likely a grant application is to be funded, or how it will score in review, before or alongside the actual review. It covers funder-specific prediction, such as forecasting panel outcomes for a given call, and cross-funder work that looks for general signals of a strong proposal. The unit of prediction is usually a single submitted proposal, though some work predicts at the level of a research team, a portfolio or a programme. It sits between bibliometrics, science of science research and the practical work of research development offices.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is proposal text, reviewer comments, panel scores, funding decisions and the metadata that surrounds them, such as applicant history, institution and prior award record. Much of this data is confidential, so work often runs on internal funder or university systems rather than open corpora, and public datasets tend to be small, redacted or limited to outcomes without full text. Models range from logistic regression and gradient boosting on structured features to transformer language models fine-tuned on abstracts and review text. Compute needs are modest compared with large language model training, and the harder constraint is data access and linkage rather than hardware.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study defines an outcome, such as fund, reject or a numeric priority score, then assembles features from the proposal, the applicant and the context. Text features come from titles, abstracts, aims pages and sometimes full narratives, while structured features capture track record, team composition, prior submissions and fit to the call. Models are trained and validated with care because funding decisions are imbalanced and clustered by panel, discipline and year, so random splits can overstate accuracy. Evaluation usually reports discrimination and calibration, and some work compares model predictions against human reviewer agreement to see whether the signal is new or merely a restatement of reviewer consensus.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Proposal text and reviews are sensitive, often containing unpublished ideas and personal information, so consent, confidentiality and data minimisation are central. Reviewers and applicants may not know that their material is being used to train a model, which raises questions about transparency and the terms under which submissions were made. There is a real risk that a model learns past bias, for example against certain institutions, career stages or topic areas, and then reproduces it at scale. Provenance matters too, since a prediction is only as good as the data behind it, and claims about accuracy should be traceable to the specific dataset, call and period rather than presented as general. Any use in a live funding process also needs a human decision point, because a model score is not a funding decision.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work is moving from predicting a binary outcome toward richer targets, such as expected review scores, likely reviewer concerns and the fit between a proposal and a specific panel. Larger language models make it easier to summarise and compare proposals, which raises the prospect of automated triage, and with it sharper questions about fairness and appeal. There is growing interest in using predictions formatively, to help applicants and research development staff improve a draft rather than to filter submissions. Progress will depend less on new architectures than on better data agreements, shared benchmarks and honest reporting of how these models behave across disciplines and funders.
